opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it was a big influence, honestly. If you go back a few years, the way most of us in the open-endedness and RL community thought about environments was that someone had to hand-design them. You'd build a simulator, a grid world, a physics engine, and then maybe you'd procedurally generate variations within that fixed space. That was the whole field of unsupervised environment design, which I'd worked on a lot. But you were always bounded by what the designer had put into the simulator in the first place.

Then text-to-image models took off. Suddenly you could type almost anything and get a plausible, often beautiful image of it. What struck me was that these models had absorbed an enormous amount of knowledge about the visual world just from internet-scale data. They weren't hand-designed for any particular domain. They were general.

So the natural question was: what if you could do the same thing, but instead of generating a single image, you generate a world you can act in? Not just a picture of a scene, but something interactive, where you press a key, take an action, and the world responds consistently. If you could do that, you'd have something like a foundation model for environments. You could generate an unlimited curriculum of worlds for agents to train in, rather than being limited to a handful of simulators someone spent years building.

That was very much the motivation behind Genie. We wanted to see whether you could learn a controllable, interactive world model purely from videos, without action labels, and then prompt it with an image, even a sketch or a photo, and step into it. Text-to-image showed us that scale and generality could produce remarkable things. The bet was that the same recipe, applied to interactive video, could give us environments that are as open-ended as the agents we eventually want to train.

r001.rationale: It frames interactive video generation as the next step after text-to-image: generating worlds people can act in, where actions change the world consistently.

r002.rationale: It describes a general foundation model that could generate an unlimited curriculum of worlds, including ones beyond the handful of hand-built simulators.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's worth going back a few years. When I started thinking about world models, the dominant paradigm was really something like Dreamer or the earlier Ha and Schmidhuber work, where you train a world model on a single environment, and the point was to use it for planning or for training a policy in imagination. And those were great, but they were narrow. You'd learn a model of one Atari game, or one MuJoCo task, and that was it.

What changed my thinking was watching what happened with text-to-image. If you go back to, say, 2020, the generative image models we had were pretty limited. You could generate faces, you could generate a specific class of thing. And then within a couple of years you had DALL-E, Imagen, Stable Diffusion, and suddenly you had a single model that could produce essentially any image you could describe. And the recipe was pretty clear in hindsight: scale the data, scale the model, use a flexible architecture, and don't constrain yourself to one domain.

So the natural question for me was, why isn't that true for world models? Why are we still training one model per environment? If you can learn a general model of what images look like from internet-scale data, you should be able to learn a general model of how worlds evolve over time, and how they respond to actions. The internet is full of video of people interacting with environments, playing games, moving through the world. That's the data.

The piece that was missing, and this is what we worked on with Genie, was the action conditioning. Text-to-image gives you a controllable generator where the control is language. For a world model you want the control to be actions, and the problem is that internet video doesn't come with action labels. So a lot of the work was figuring out how to learn a latent action space in an unsupervised way, so the model could discover for itself what the controllable factors were, and then you get something that behaves like a game engine you can step through, trained entirely from unlabeled video.

And I think the broader lesson I took from text-to-image was about ambition, honestly. People were skeptical that a single image model could be general, and then it just was. So I became a lot more comfortable saying: let's not build a world model for one environment, let's try to build a foundation world model, in the same sense that we talk about foundation language models, and see how far the scaling story carries us.

r001.rationale: The response discusses text-to-image progress and using internet video to train world models, but does not present video generation as an intermediate step toward world models.

r002.rationale: It contrasts one-model-per-environment approaches with a general foundation world model, but does not clearly state that the model is intended to simulate arbitrary environments, including new ones.

astra-6.text:
The progress in text-to-image models gave us a really compelling example of what happens when you move from training a model for one narrow setting to training on a broad distribution of data. You have this single model that can generate an enormous variety of scenes, and language becomes a way to specify what you want.

The question for us was: could we do something similar for world models? Instead of learning a model of one particular environment, could we learn a model across many environments that you could then use to create something new?

The key difference is that a world needs to be interactive. It’s not enough to generate a beautiful image, or even a plausible video. If an agent takes an action, the world needs to respond to that action. So the idea of a foundation world model was to bring that breadth of generative capability together with action-conditioned dynamics—to generate environments that an agent can actually interact with and learn in.

r001.rationale: The response says plausible video is insufficient and moves from broad image generation to interactive world models. It does not present video generation as an intermediate step toward world models.

r002.rationale: It contrasts modeling one particular environment with learning across many environments to create something new, conveying the intended ability to model new environments.

sol-6.1.text:
The progress in text-to-image models made us ask whether we could do something similar for interactive worlds. You can describe an image in natural language and get something incredibly rich and varied. What if you could describe an environment, generate it, and then actually act within it?

That’s the idea behind a foundation world model: a model that can generate a broad range of environments and simulate how they respond to actions. Instead of producing a single image, it needs to keep generating what happens next as an agent interacts with the world. And that opens up a really exciting possibility for training agents, because you could give them a much wider variety of experiences than you could by building every environment by hand.

r001.rationale: The response moves from generating a single image to generating what happens as an agent interacts with a world, but it does not identify video generation as an intermediate step.

r002.rationale: It says a foundation world model can generate a broad range of environments, but does not clearly state that it can simulate arbitrary or new environments, in contrast to an environment-specific model.
